title: Lift each gnocchi out of simmering water with a slotted spoon soon after it floats up, then turn off the burner
instruction: The gnocchi are cooking. Take them out onto the plate when they're done, then turn off the burner.
context: Restaurant cooks (O*NET 35-2014.00, about 1.4 million US jobs) cook pasta and dumplings to order, and O*NET lists their task "Observe and test foods to determine if they have been cooked sufficiently". Fresh potato gnocchi sink raw and float up when cooked through, 1 1/2 to 2 minutes after going in (America's Test Kitchen), and the cook lifts each one out with a slotted spoon as it comes up. Pieces go in at different times and surface seconds apart, so the cook watches the pan and takes each in turn, without pushing the floater away or catching raw ones still on the floor. One taken out early is raw in the middle; one left floating goes soft. Cooked gnocchi are soft, so they are lifted in the spoon, never pinched. The cooking step ends with the heat off: once the last piece is out, the cook turns the burner off rather than leave the pan simmering unattended, and the station is left safe. It is the finish of the same job, not a separate appliance task.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. Induction hob: a slim portable single-zone hob, black glass top, 36 cm deep x 28 cm wide x 4 cm tall, centered at x 30, y 2; fixed. Burner knob: the hob's rotary control, a black range knob 4.2 cm across and 2.6 cm tall with a grip bar 3.6 cm long and 9 mm thick across its top and a white pointer, on the hob's top in its near-left corner at x 14.5, y 12.5. It turns clockwise from OFF (pointer toward the robot, also its stop) to HIGH at 300 degrees, with about 0.1 N m of friction and a click into OFF, and starts at 90 degrees, the low-medium setting that keeps the water at a gentle simmer. Pan: a 24 cm stainless saute pan, inside 24 cm across and 7 cm deep with a 5 mm base, centered at x 30, y 2 (inside floor at z 4.5, rim at z 11.5), its long handle pointing away from the robot; fixed. Water: 2.4 L, 5.3 cm deep, surface at z 9.8. Gnocchi G1-G6: fresh potato gnocchi, ridged pillows 2.3 cm long, 1.5 cm across and 1.1 cm thick, 3.0 g each (dough at 1.08 g/cm3), lying on the pan floor in a ring 4.5 cm out from its center on the half nearer the right arm, long side along the ring, at (x, y) = (27.8, 5.9), (25.8, 3.5), (25.8, 0.5), (27.8, -1.9), (30.8, -2.4), (33.4, -0.9). They go into the water two at a time, 85, 57 and 30 s before the trial starts, and each floats up 1 1/2 to 2 minutes after it goes in: in the canonical run at about 10.5, 21.5, 38.5, 49.5, 65.5 and 78.5 s, so the second of each pair comes up while the first is on its way to the plate. Other runs share the pieces among the three drops at random and draw each floating time anew within 1 1/2 to 2 minutes. Slotted spoon: a black nylon slotted spoon 32 cm long, 80 g: bowl 8 x 6 cm, 1.2 cm deep at the back, its sides 8 mm and its front edge flush with its floor, with nine 3 x 25 mm slots; a 24 cm handle rising 30 degrees from the bowl's plane, a 1.5 cm-wide neck, then a soft grip 2.8 cm wide and 1.8 cm thick. It lies on the counter right of the hob as it was put down, on the back of its bowl and the end of its handle, the bowl's middle at x 31, y -28, the handle pointing away from the robot and nearly flat, the bowl tipped up 27 degrees; loose. Plate: a white ceramic plate 18 cm across, its flat well 14 cm across and 6 mm up, its rim rising to 2 cm, centered at x 16.5, y -25.5; fixed (a damp cloth under it). Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: A piece has floated up when its top is within 3 mm of the water's surface on its own (a cooked gnocchi floats with about 1 mm showing), not resting in the spoon. It is out when its lowest point last rose above the surface. It is good when it came out after it floated up and no more than 45 s later (cooks lift them as they come up; left floating they go soft), it ends on the plate and still for 1 s (center over the 14 cm well, lowest point at most 2 cm above it, not in the spoon), and no gripper ever touched it (a contact check of the hand's own palm, fingers and pads, not a distance zone: a pinch dents a soft cooked gnocchi). The burner is off when the knob's pointer is within 8 degrees of OFF, inside its click. The trial scores 1.0 when all six pieces are good, no hand is on the spoon and the burner is off. It scores 0.75 with five good pieces, 0.5 with three or four and 0.25 with one or two. A hand still on the spoon at the end caps the score at 0.5, because the spoon was not put down, and so does the burner left on, because the cooking step is not finished while the pan is left simmering unattended (how kitchen fires start). The whole trial scores 0 if any piece ends outside the pan without having floated up before it left the water: a raw gnocchi was served, wherever it was put. Otherwise it scores 0, including when nothing is done (every piece goes soft in the water). Scooping everything out early scores 0; leaving them all and scooping them in the last 10 s of the run scores 0.25 at most. Turning the burner off with no piece plated scores 0. The burner may be turned off at any time; the spoon may end anywhere and no arm position is scored. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. Real trial: an overhead video at 30 fps gives each piece's floating and out times, read frame by frame; the final photo shows the plate and the knob's pointer; a piece touched by a finger shows on the wrist video and is visibly dented; a piece suspected raw is cut open (a raw center is dense and floury).
reset_notes: The gnocchi are consumed: use six fresh ones of the same batch each trial (2.3 x 1.5 x 1.1 cm, 3 g, checked on a kitchen scale). Top the pan back up to 2.4 L, turn the knob back to 90 degrees, bring the water back to a gentle simmer and lay the spoon back on its tape mark. The operator drops the gnocchi in two at a time, 85, 57 and 30 s before the start, from a long-handled spoon at the pan's far side, outside the arms' reach; each piece's 45 s is measured from its own floating time on the video.
fidelity: Water is not simulated: a model adds buoyancy from each piece's submerged volume, drag, a gentle simmer drift and the moving spoon's push; the surface is flat. Gnocchi are rigid pillows that turn buoyant at set times, as if cooked through. The spoon drains as if fully slotted. Nothing is hot: only the knob's setting is scored; the water simmers on after it is off. A pinch is scored by contact, not modeled as a dent. Hob, pan and plate are fixed; the real pan, about 3.5 kg filled, stands loose.
